title: AI and prompt injections: the invoice that approves itself.
summary: This post demonstrates how prompt injection attacks can exploit AI document processing pipelines in Business Central, where hidden text in PDFs manipulates invoice data and approval status, and presents a layered defense strategy including invisible text detection, image-based analysis, strict schemas, and deterministic validation.
key_points: Indirect prompt injection occurs when untrusted documents contain hidden instructions that manipulate AI model behavior, posing risk to invoice processing and payment automation
PDFs are effective attack vectors because text extractors capture invisible content (white text, tiny fonts, hidden metadata) that humans cannot see
A vulnerable pipeline allows the AI model to extract data, make approval decisions, and directly influence business transactions without validation

Defense requires five layered controls: hidden text detection, rendering pages as images for vision models, strict output schemas, removing decision fields, and deterministic validation against master data
The architecture and design determine security more than the prompt; payment decisions must come from internal workflow and verified data, never from document content

quotes.text: Your AI will believe anything a document tells it. Build a system that doesn't.
quotes.why_it_matters: Core principle: security must be in the system design and architecture, not relying on AI behavior or prompts alone

quotes.text: Prompt injection isn't a bug you patch in the prompt. It's a trust problem you solve in the design.
quotes.why_it_matters: Reframes the security challenge as an architectural issue requiring deterministic controls, not just better instructions
